title: Network of Theseus (Like the ship)
claim: A model can be converted into a different architecture by incrementally swapping each part for a target module aligned by representational similarity.
layout: 2 steps, left-to-right, columns of progressively swapped layers with dotted loss arrows
description: A two-step diagram titled "Building the Network of Theseus" with a small sailboat emoji. Step 1, "Progressive Layer Replacement", is a row of vertical four-layer stacks. The far-left gray box, "Original Network", holds teal squares. Three columns labeled Patch 1, 2 and 3 replace the teal squares with orange circles from the bottom up, one more layer each time. The far-right gray box, "Target Network", is all orange circles. Dotted horizontal arrows labeled ℓ_SIM link each new orange circle to the corresponding original or previous layer. Each stack takes input x at the bottom. Step 2, "Standard Training", is a separate panel with an all-orange target network. It has a dotted arrow from label y marked ℓ_TRAIN. The teal-to-orange color change draws the eye first.
caption: Network of Theseus. A network can be converted to any desired target network by replacing each piece of the original network incrementally, part-by-part. Each original part is replaced by optimizing the representational alignment, ℓSIM, of the target part to the original part. After all original parts are replaced, only the target network remains and can be trained on any downstream task (i.e. standard training).
abstract: A standard assumption in deep learning is that the inductive bias introduced by a neural network architecture must persist from training through inference. The architecture you train with is the architecture you deploy. This assumption constrains the community from selecting architectures that may have desirable efficiency or design properties due to difficulties with optimization. We challenge this assumption with the Network of Theseus (NoT), a method for progressively converting a trained, or even untrained, guide network architecture part-by-part into an entirely different target network architecture while preserving the performance of the guide network. At each stage, components in the guide network architecture are incrementally replaced with the target architecture modules and aligned via representational similarity metrics. This procedure preserves most of the functionality of the guide network even under substantial architectural changes-for example, converting a convolutional network into a multilayer perceptron, or GPT-2 into a recurrent neural network. By decoupling optimization from deployment, NoT expands the space of viable inference-time architectures, opening opportunities for better accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs and enabling more directed exploration of the architectural design space.
